reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight of the paper lies in treating peak age as a latent variable derived from underlying performance trajectories, rather than a direct observation. This requires a dual modeling approach: one for reconstructing the noisy longitudinal performance data, and another for inferring the latent maximizer. The longitudinal model assumes that observed performances are noisy realizations of smooth, latent performance functions, modeled via Gaussian processes or splines. The peak age is then defined as the argmax of this trajectory. To make this inference robust, the authors employ a hierarchical Bayesian framework that accounts for inter-individual variability and allows borrowing strength across athletes. The peak-age component further embeds this latent variable into an accelerated failure time (AFT) model, linking it to athlete-level covariates such as sport discipline or training background. This dualism—trajectory modeling and latent peak inference—is essential for handling incomplete and irregular observation windows typical in sports analytics. The joint inference ensures that uncertainty in trajectory reconstruction propagates correctly into peak age estimation and regression analysis. Simulations demonstrate that this approach reduces bias compared to pseudo-peak methods or two-stage estimators, especially under low-information regimes. The framework thus provides a principled way to estimate age-of-peak performance with quantified uncertainty, supporting applications in talent identification, training design, and comparative sports science.
